addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	import Foundation

3	/// The full result of a short status command: stdout, stderr, exit code, and whether the
4	/// timeout fired. Unlike `CommandRunning` (which collapses everything to `String?`), this
5	/// keeps the exit code and timeout flag so `WorkroomStatusResolver` can tell "not a repo"
6	/// (git exit 128) from "gh not installed" (exit 127) from "timed out" from "clean" — the
7	/// distinctions the status UI's unknown/stale/absent matrix depends on.
8	struct CommandResult: Sendable, Equatable {
9	  let stdout: String
10	  let stderr: String
11	  let exitCode: Int32
12	  let timedOut: Bool
13	
14	  /// `/usr/bin/env` exits 127 when the command (git/jj/gh) isn't on PATH.
15	  static let commandNotFound: Int32 = 127
16	  /// git exits 128 for "not a git repository" and similar fatal usage errors.
17	  static let gitFatal: Int32 = 128
18	
19	  var ok: Bool { exitCode == 0 && !timedOut }
20	}
21	
22	/// A seam (mirrors `CommandRunning`) so `WorkroomStatusResolver` is unit-testable without
23	/// spawning real git/jj/gh — but typed (`CommandResult`, not `String?`).
24	protocol StatusCommandRunning: Sendable {
25	  func run(_ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String, timeout: TimeInterval)
26	    async -> CommandResult
27	
28	  /// Like `run`, but feeds `stdin` to the child on its standard input.
29	  ///
30	  /// Exists for the commit path, where passing data as **argv is either unsafe or impossible**:
31	  /// - `git add --pathspec-from-file=- --pathspec-file-nul` takes the selected paths NUL-separated
32	  ///   on stdin. That is the only form git treats pathspecs as **literal** — after a bare `--` they
33	  ///   are still glob magic, so selecting `a[b].txt` also stages `ab.txt` (measured), and a file
34	  ///   named `*` stages the whole tree. It also sidesteps `E2BIG`, which a few thousand long paths
35	  ///   in `proc.arguments` would hit at spawn, before git can emit anything classifiable.
36	  /// - `git commit --file=-` takes the message on stdin, so no length or encoding question arises.
37	  ///
38	  /// A per-call **environment** override is deliberately NOT added yet: its only planned consumer is
39	  /// `GIT_INDEX_FILE` for temp-index commits, which is deferred, and an unused parameter is surface
40	  /// nobody can test.
41	  func run(
42	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String, timeout: TimeInterval,
43	    stdin: Data?
44	  ) async -> CommandResult
45	
46	  /// Like `run`, but for a command that will touch the **network** and therefore may want to
47	  /// authenticate — `git fetch/push/pull`, `jj git fetch/push`.
48	  ///
49	  /// A read like `git status` can never prompt, so it wants the minimal, predictable environment
50	  /// `run` gives it. A push can: it may need an SSH agent the GUI environment can't see, and it may
51	  /// try to ask for a passphrase or a host-key confirmation with nowhere to ask. See
52	  /// `StatusCommandRunner.networkEnvironment` for what changes and why.
53	  func runNetwork(
54	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String,
55	    timeout: TimeInterval
56	  ) async -> CommandResult
57	}
58	
59	extension StatusCommandRunning {
60	  /// Test doubles never reach a real network, so the distinction is meaningless for them — forward
61	  /// and let them stay two-line stubs. Only `StatusCommandRunner` overrides this.
62	  func runNetwork(
63	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String,
64	    timeout: TimeInterval
65	  ) async -> CommandResult {
66	    await run(executable, args, in: directory, timeout: timeout)
67	  }
68	
69	  /// Same reasoning as `runNetwork`: a double that records argv doesn't care about the payload, so
70	  /// it stays a two-line stub. A double that DOES need to assert on stdin (the commit tests) can
71	  /// override this one method. Only `StatusCommandRunner` writes a real pipe.
72	  func run(
73	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String, timeout: TimeInterval,
74	    stdin: Data?
75	  ) async -> CommandResult {
76	    await run(executable, args, in: directory, timeout: timeout)
77	  }
78	}

80	/// Default `StatusCommandRunning`: spawns via `/usr/bin/env` (augmented PATH finds Homebrew
81	/// git/jj/gh), git locks/prompt disabled, and enforces `timeout` by terminating the process.
82	///
83	/// Unlike `ProcessCommandRunner` (which reads stdout *in* the termination handler — safe only
84	/// because a branch name is tiny), this drains stdout AND stderr **concurrently on background
85	/// queues while the process runs** (the `WorkroomCLI` pattern). Status output can be large (a
86	/// repo with thousands of changed files, a big `gh` JSON payload); reading post-termination
87	/// would let the OS pipe buffer fill, block the child on write, and deadlock until the timeout.
88	/// Retained output is capped (`maxBytes`) so a pathological repo can't blow memory — the reader
89	/// keeps draining past the cap (so the child never blocks) but discards the overflow.
90	struct StatusCommandRunner: StatusCommandRunning, Sendable {
91	  var maxBytes: Int = 4 * 1024 * 1024
92	
93	  /// Auth-relevant variables forwarded from the user's shell for network commands only.
94	  ///
95	  /// A Finder- or Dock-launched `.app` inherits launchd's environment, not the user's shell, and this
96	  /// runner otherwise overrides only PATH. That was harmless while it ran `git status` and `gh` (which
97	  /// carries its own token), but it breaks authentication outright: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is how a process
98	  /// finds an SSH agent, and for anyone using 1Password's agent, gpg-agent, or a custom socket it is
99	  /// set in `.zshrc` and nowhere else. Without it their `git push` cannot reach the agent, and the
100	  /// error would tell them to configure a credential helper they already have.
101	  ///
102	  /// Deliberately an allowlist, not the whole probed environment (which `ShellEnvironment.environment()`
103	  /// hands to setup/teardown scripts): network ops now run automatically on inspector focus, and a
104	  /// wholesale transplant would put every variable in the user's shell — secrets included — into a
105	  /// child on an automatic path.
106	  static let forwardedAuthKeys = [
107	    "SSH_AUTH_SOCK", "SSH_AGENT_PID", "GIT_SSH_COMMAND", "GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL", "XDG_CONFIG_HOME",
108	  ]
109	
110	  /// Variables removed for network commands so `ssh` cannot find a graphical prompt helper.
111	  static let networkClearedKeys = ["SSH_ASKPASS", "DISPLAY"]
112	
113	  /// The environment for a network command: `base` plus forwarded auth vars, with ssh pinned to
114	  /// fail fast instead of asking a human.
115	  ///
116	  /// `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` (set by `run`) governs **git's own** credential prompts and says nothing
117	  /// to `ssh`. So an SSH remote with a passphrase-protected key and no agent, or a host whose key
118	  /// isn't in `known_hosts`, would otherwise stall until the timeout — 120s for fetch/push, 300s for
119	  /// pull. `BatchMode=yes` turns both into an immediate, classifiable failure, and
120	  /// `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=never` stops ssh reaching for a GUI helper (OpenSSH 8.4+; macOS ships 10.x).
121	  ///
122	  /// A user's own `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` is preserved and appended to rather than replaced — it commonly
123	  /// carries `-i <key>` or a proxy command that must survive.
124	  ///
125	  /// Pure and static so the whole policy is unit-testable without spawning anything.
126	  static func networkEnvironment(base: [String: String], probed: [String: String])
127	    -> [String: String]
128	  {
129	    var env = base
130	    for key in forwardedAuthKeys {
131	      // The inherited environment wins: if it's already set, the app was launched from a shell that
132	      // had it, and that value is at least as current as the probe's.
133	      if env[key] == nil, let value = probed[key], !value.isEmpty { env[key] = value }
134	    }
135	    for key in networkClearedKeys { env.removeValue(forKey: key) }
136	    let ssh = env["GIT_SSH_COMMAND"]?.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
137	    env["GIT_SSH_COMMAND"] = (ssh?.isEmpty == false ? ssh! : "ssh") + " -o BatchMode=yes"
138	    env["SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE"] = "never"
139	    return env
140	  }
141	
142	  func run(_ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String, timeout: TimeInterval)
143	    async -> CommandResult
144	  {
145	    await run(executable, args, in: directory, timeout: timeout, network: false, stdin: nil)
146	  }
147	
148	  func run(
149	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String, timeout: TimeInterval,
150	    stdin: Data?
151	  ) async -> CommandResult {
152	    await run(executable, args, in: directory, timeout: timeout, network: false, stdin: stdin)
153	  }
154	
155	  func runNetwork(
156	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String,
157	    timeout: TimeInterval
158	  ) async -> CommandResult {
159	    await run(executable, args, in: directory, timeout: timeout, network: true, stdin: nil)
160	  }
161	
162	  private func run(
163	    _ executable: String, _ args: [String], in directory: String,
164	    timeout: TimeInterval, network: Bool, stdin: Data?
165	  ) async -> CommandResult {
166	    let proc = Process()
167	    proc.executableURL = URL(fileURLWithPath: "/usr/bin/env")
168	    proc.arguments = [executable] + args
169	    proc.currentDirectoryURL = URL(fileURLWithPath: directory)
170	
171	    var env = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment
172	    env["PATH"] = ShellEnvironment.path()
173	    env["GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS"] = "0"
174	    env["GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT"] = "0"
175	    // Pin the message locale: EVERY consumer of this runner classifies failures by matching English
176	    // substrings of git's stderr (`CLIVCSWriter.classify`, `WorkroomStatusResolver`), and git ships
177	    // translated message catalogs. Homebrew git 2.55 under a French locale answers
178	    // `erreur : le spécificateur de chemin …`, so without this a non-English user loses the ENTIRE
179	    // failure taxonomy at once — auth, host-key, rejected-push, dirty-tree and leftover-lock all
180	    // collapse to `.other(rawStderr)` with no recovery offered.
181	    //
182	    // `LC_ALL`, not `LC_MESSAGES`: this env is seeded from `ProcessInfo.environment`, so the user's own
183	    // `LC_ALL` may be inherited, and it OUTRANKS `LC_MESSAGES` — setting the narrower variable is
184	    // silently defeated (measured: `LC_ALL=fr_FR.UTF-8 LC_MESSAGES=C git …` still answers in French).
185	    //
186	    // Safe for paths despite forcing the C charset: git writes pathnames as raw bytes (and quotes
187	    // non-ASCII per `core.quotePath` regardless of locale), so `LC_ALL=C` renders a `café-ünï.txt`
188	    // byte-identically to the user's own locale — verified, not assumed. jj and gh are unaffected
189	    // either way; neither localizes.
190	    env["LC_ALL"] = "C"
191	    // A workroom can be a clone of an *untrusted* repo, and the status sweep runs git automatically
192	    // on load/focus/selection. `git diff` would otherwise run an inherited external-diff program;
193	    // unset it so only the explicit `--no-ext-diff` flag (see WorkroomStatusResolver) governs diffs.
194	    env.removeValue(forKey: "GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF")
195	    if network { env = Self.networkEnvironment(base: env, probed: ShellEnvironment.environment()) }
196	    proc.environment = env
197	
198	    let outPipe = Pipe()
199	    let errPipe = Pipe()
200	    proc.standardOutput = outPipe
201	    proc.standardError = errPipe
202	    // Never let a child read the app's stdin. Unset, it INHERITS ours — which under `make app-run`
203	    // (or `Scripts/run.sh`) is a real terminal, so a prompting `ssh` or `git` could sit waiting on a
204	    // tty that the same binary won't have when launched from Finder. Pinning it makes the two launch
205	    // contexts behave identically and turns any prompt into an immediate EOF. `ShellEnvironment.probe`
206	    // already does this for the same reason.
207	    //
208	    // A caller-supplied payload replaces the null device with a pipe we write and then close, so the
209	    // child still sees a clean EOF and can never wait on a human.
210	    let inPipe: Pipe? = stdin == nil ? nil : Pipe()
211	    proc.standardInput = inPipe ?? FileHandle.nullDevice
212	
213	    // `proc` is shared with the @Sendable cancellation handler; box it so the non-Sendable Process
214	    // can cross that boundary (mirrors the @unchecked Sendable helpers below).
215	    let box = ProcessBox(proc)
216	
217	    return await withTaskCancellationHandler {
218	      await withCheckedContinuation { (continuation: CheckedContinuation<CommandResult, Never>) in
219	        let state = StatusRunState()
220	        let drain = DispatchGroup()
221	        let cap = maxBytes
222	        let gate = CommandResumeGate(continuation)
223	
224	        // Concurrent drains (the deadlock fix). availableData blocks until data or EOF;
225	        // started before run() so we never miss a fast child's output, harmless until it runs.
226	        drain.enter()
227	        DispatchQueue.global().async {
228	          state.setStdout(Self.readCapped(outPipe.fileHandleForReading, cap: cap))
229	          drain.leave()
230	        }
231	        drain.enter()
232	        DispatchQueue.global().async {
233	          state.setStderr(Self.readCapped(errPipe.fileHandleForReading, cap: cap))
234	          drain.leave()
235	        }
236	
237	        let timeoutItem = DispatchWorkItem {
238	          state.markTimedOut()
239	          if proc.isRunning { proc.terminate() }  // SIGTERM
240	        }
241	        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + timeout, execute: timeoutItem)
242	
243	        // Hard-kill fallback: a wedged child (e.g. `gh` blocked on a dead socket) can ignore SIGTERM,
244	        // so `terminationHandler` — the only place the continuation resumes — would never fire and the
245	        // awaiting Task would hang forever, defeating the timeout. SIGKILL is uncatchable, guaranteeing
246	        // the process exits and we resume. A 2s grace after SIGTERM lets well-behaved children exit.
247	        let killItem = DispatchWorkItem {
248	          if proc.isRunning { ProcessTree.killTree(proc.processIdentifier) }
249	        }
250	        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + timeout + 2, execute: killItem)
251	
252	        proc.terminationHandler = { finished in
253	          timeoutItem.cancel()
254	          killItem.cancel()
255	          // The process has exited, so its own pipe write ends are closed and EOF is imminent. But a
256	          // grandchild that inherited the pipe (a helper spawned by gh/git) can hold the write end
257	          // open after the parent dies — an unbounded `drain.wait()` would then never return and the
258	          // continuation would never resume, wedging this probe slot forever. Bound the wait and
259	          // resume with whatever drained; a still-blocked reader writes to `state` we no longer read
260	          // (safe — lock-guarded) and exits when the grandchild finally closes the pipe.
261	          _ = drain.wait(timeout: .now() + 2)
262	          gate.resume(
263	            CommandResult(
264	              stdout: String(decoding: state.stdout, as: UTF8.self),
265	              stderr: String(decoding: state.stderr, as: UTF8.self),
266	              exitCode: finished.terminationStatus,
267	              timedOut: state.timedOut))
268	        }
269	
270	        do {
271	          try proc.run()
272	          // Feed stdin AFTER the child exists, on a background queue, and close to signal EOF.
273	          // Off the calling thread because a payload larger than the 64K pipe buffer blocks until
274	          // the child drains it, and `git` does not start reading until it has parsed its argv.
275	          if let inPipe, let payload = stdin {
276	            DispatchQueue.global().async {
277	              let handle = inPipe.fileHandleForWriting
278	              // Darwin's per-descriptor SIGPIPE suppression. Without it, a child that exits before
279	              // reading (git rejecting its argv, a hook killing it) makes our `write(2)` raise
280	              // SIGPIPE, whose default disposition TERMINATES the app — a crash reachable from an
281	              // ordinary failed commit. With it the write just returns EPIPE, which `try?` drops.
282	              _ = fcntl(handle.fileDescriptor, F_SETNOSIGPIPE, 1)
283	              if !payload.isEmpty { try? handle.write(contentsOf: payload) }
284	              try? handle.close()
285	            }
286	          }
287	        } catch {
288	          // Launch failed (e.g. cwd vanished). Close the write ends so the drain readers hit
289	          // EOF instead of blocking forever, then resolve as command-not-found.
290	          timeoutItem.cancel()
291	          killItem.cancel()
292	          try? inPipe?.fileHandleForWriting.close()
293	          try? outPipe.fileHandleForWriting.close()
294	          try? errPipe.fileHandleForWriting.close()
295	          gate.resume(
296	            CommandResult(
297	              stdout: "", stderr: "\(error)", exitCode: CommandResult.commandNotFound,
298	              timedOut: false))
299	        }
300	      }
301	    } onCancel: {
302	      // The awaiting Task was cancelled (e.g. a superseded sweep, or rapid selection cycling). Kill
303	      // the in-flight child so a cancelled probe doesn't leave a git/jj/gh process running to its own
304	      // timeout. terminationHandler then resumes the continuation with the abandoned result, which
305	      // the cancelled caller discards. SIGKILL (not SIGTERM) so a wedged child dies promptly.
306	      box.terminate()
307	    }
308	  }
309	
310	  /// Drain a pipe to EOF, retaining at most `cap` bytes but reading the rest so the child
311	  /// never blocks on a full pipe buffer.
312	  private static func readCapped(_ handle: FileHandle, cap: Int) -> Data {
313	    var collected = Data()
314	    while true {
315	      // `read(upToCount:)` (throwing) instead of `availableData`: the latter raises an
316	      // *Objective-C* `NSFileHandleOperationException` on a read error (common right after the
317	      // child is `terminate()`d out from under the open read end), which Swift can't catch — it
318	      // crashes the app. Treat a read error as EOF and return what we have.
319	      let chunk: Data
320	      do { chunk = try handle.read(upToCount: 1 << 16) ?? Data() } catch { break }
321	      if chunk.isEmpty { break }  // EOF: pipe closed
322	      if collected.count < cap {
323	        collected.append(chunk.prefix(cap - collected.count))
324	      }
325	    }
326	    return collected
327	  }
328	}

330	/// Boxes a non-Sendable `Process` so it can be captured by the @Sendable task-cancellation handler.
331	private final class ProcessBox: @unchecked Sendable {
332	  private let process: Process
333	  init(_ process: Process) { self.process = process }
334	  /// SIGKILL the child (and any descendants it spawned) if still running — the cancellation path
335	  /// abandons the result, so kill promptly rather than wait out a SIGTERM grace.
336	  ///
337	  /// Hopped to a global queue because `withTaskCancellationHandler`'s `onCancel` runs **synchronously
338	  /// on whichever thread called `cancel()`**, and the hottest canceller is the main thread:
339	  /// `selectedTargetID.didSet` → `scheduleSelectedStatusRefresh` → `selectionStatusTask?.cancel()`
340	  /// supersedes the in-flight probe on *every* selection change. `ProcessTree.killTree` walks the tree
341	  /// by spawning a `pgrep -P` per node and blocking on `waitUntilExit` for each, so inline it stalled
342	  /// the main thread for the length of that walk while switching workroom tabs — and a blocking wait
343	  /// spins a nested run loop, which drains queued main-queue blocks at a point SwiftUI hasn't committed
344	  /// its update yet (that reordering is what surfaced the split-member selection snap-back). Deferring
345	  /// the kill costs nothing: the continuation resumes from `terminationHandler`, never from here, and
346	  /// the cancelled caller discards the result. Matches `killItem`, which already kills off a global
347	  /// queue.
348	  func terminate() {
349	    let process = self.process
350	    DispatchQueue.global(qos: .userInitiated).async {
351	      if process.isRunning { ProcessTree.killTree(process.processIdentifier) }
352	    }
353	  }
354	}
355	
356	/// Mutable scratch shared between the drain queues and the termination handler. Locked
357	/// because the two reads and the handler touch it from different threads.
358	private final class StatusRunState: @unchecked Sendable {
359	  private let lock = NSLock()
360	  private var _stdout = Data()
361	  private var _stderr = Data()
362	  private var _timedOut = false
363	
364	  func setStdout(_ d: Data) {
365	    lock.lock()
366	    _stdout = d

content.text:
Based on my thorough review, I've examined:

**Sinks introduced:**
- `Process` subprocess execution for `git commit`/`jj commit`/`jj describe`
- `stdin` pipe write for pathspec payload
- File I/O for sequencer marker detection

**Data flow traced:**
- **Commit message** (`summary`+`messageBody`): user input → `-m <value>` argv element. Passed to `Process` directly (not via shell), so shell metacharacters are inert. `-m` consumes the next argv unconditionally, so a message starting with `-` cannot be reinterpreted as an option.
- **Pathspec payload**: file paths from trusted `WorkroomStatus` → NUL-separated, `:(literal)`-prefixed, written to stdin. The `:(literal)` prefix (verified by tests) neutralizes glob magic that `--pathspec-file-nul` does NOT disable — the exact bug the "unanchored allowlist" pattern would flag is *prevented* here.
- **Working directory** (`path`): from app-owned `StatusWorkItem`, not attacker-influenceable.
- **Rename entries**: correctly consume the extra NUL field in porcelain parsing (`stagedContentAtRisk`), preventing desync — explicitly tested.

**Fail-safety:**
- `SIGPIPE` handled via `F_SETNOSIGPIPE`, preventing app-crash-from-failed-commit.
- Locale pinned to `C` (`LC_ALL=C`) so classification cannot be locale-dodged.
- `stagedContentAtRisk` fail-open is documented as an informational guard, not a security control — losing staged content is a data-loss/UX concern, not an authorization bypass.
- Per-project gate wraps the commit sequence atomically; `isCommitting` suppresses concurrent status probes across three lanes (timer refresh, selection refresh, FSEvents watcher).

**Classification robustness:**
- Hook rejection uses explicit marker allowlist, not catch-all — verified by test `testUnmatchedFailuresStayOtherRatherThanBecomingHookRejections`.
- `sequencerState` correctly orders cherry-pick/revert BEFORE merge (both leave `MERGE_HEAD`), so users are sent to finish the right operation.

**No credential/PII observability sinks** introduced — commit messages and stderr are surfaced only to the local user in the sheet.

**Not security-relevant** (already noted in comments as intentional design):
- `before`/`after` revision comparison outside the gate could false-positive `.committedThenFailed` if an external terminal commits during a hook-rejected commit — this is a UX/data-integrity concern, not a security bypass.
- Marker substring matching against `err.contains` could misclassify hostile filenames — no security impact since output is local.

The change is defensively engineered against the classic pitfalls in this problem space (glob injection via pathspec, `E2BIG`, SIGPIPE crash, locale-dependent classification, snapshot-during-write races). I found no exploitable vulnerabilities.
